title: Normalize each token across its own features

blocks.text: The central question is which entries contribute to the mean and variance. Layer normalization for this exercise uses the last axis only. Two neighboring tokens can have very different scales, and each is normalized using its own feature vector. The batch and sequence axes are not pooled together.

Implement a function to perform Layer Normalization on an input tensor. Given a 3D array representing batch_size, sequence length, and feature dimensions, normalize the data across the feature dimension for each sequence, then apply scaling and shifting parameters.

A sequence tensor commonly has shape (batch, tokens, features). An axis specifies which entries are grouped by a reduction. Layer normalization computes statistics over features for each batch/token position. Gamma and beta are learned per-feature scale and shift parameters.

The example uses [1,2,3] and [10,20,30]. Their means and variances differ, but after centering and scaling they have nearly the same normalized pattern. The small difference comes from adding the same epsilon to two different variances. Keeping the reduced axis as size one ensures that each mean and scale broadcasts back to the correct token.

blocks.text: Connect the picture to the mathematics

blocks.caption: d is the feature count, epsilon is a small positive stabilizer, and gamma/beta broadcast along batch and token axes.

blocks.text: Gamma and beta operate after normalization. Change the scenario to give features different scales and offsets. The final outputs no longer need to have zero mean or unit variance; that is expected. The affine parameters allow the model to adjust the representation while the normalization stabilizes the statistics entering that adjustment.

The supplied code uses NumPy population variance, dividing squared deviations by d rather than d−1. This is the normalization convention, not an unbiased estimate of a population variance from samples. A constant token vector has zero centered features and therefore normalizes to zeros before beta is added. Epsilon protects the denominator. Common errors include reducing over the sequence axis, forgetting keepdims, or assuming gamma is one scalar rather than a feature vector. Check shapes and per-token statistics before examining final learned-affine outputs.

q233-new-case.prompt: A token is constant [5,5,5] and beta is [1,1,1]. What is each final output value, regardless of finite gamma?

explanation.correct: Centering gives zeros, normalization keeps zeros, and adding beta yields ones.
explanation.default: Revisit the stated quantities and units. Centering gives zeros, normalization keeps zeros, and adding beta yields ones.

q233-prediction.prompt: A token has features [1,2,3]. What mean is subtracted from each feature?

explanation.default: Revisit the stated quantities and units. The per-token feature mean is (1+2+3)/3=2.
